title: Diffuse and specular — Image Wiki
text:
Diffuse and specular
  Light hitting a surface either goes in and comes back out coloured, or bounces straight off keeping the light's own colour. Almost everything a material looks like follows from the split between those two.

  
    Termdiffuse reflection / specular reflection
    Also calledmatte and shiny, body colour and highlight, Lambertian reflection, gloss
    Not the same asroughness, albedo, a highlight vs a light-coloured patch of paint
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensWhat you can see in the pictureAcross different mediaCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Put a green apple under a kitchen lamp and look at it. The apple is green — all over, on the top, on the side, in the part rolling into shadow. And somewhere on it there is a small bright spot that is not green. It is white, and if you squint you can see that it has the shape of the lamp.
Two things are happening on that one piece of skin, and they barely interact. The green is diffuse reflection. The white spot is specular reflection. Almost everything you can say about what a material looks like comes out of the balance between them.
Why it happens
When light arrives at a surface it takes one of two routes.

eye 1eye 2scattered insideout in every directionDiffusematte paint, chalk, unglazed claysame brightness from anywhereeye 1eye 2θθangle in = angle outthe highlight moves with the eyeSpecularthe highlight — an image of the lampmoves when the viewer moves

Left — the diffuse route. The ray crosses the boundary, is scattered by whatever the material is made of, and leaves in a direction unrelated to where it came from. Both eyes are fed by the same outgoing fan: move, and nothing changes.
Right — the specular route. Same ray, same surface, but the bounce happens at the boundary, at the mirror angle. There is one outgoing direction per incoming one, so eye 1 sees a bright point only where that condition is met. Move to eye 2 and it is met somewhere else — the faint second pair of rays. The highlight has moved; the shading has not.


Route one, going in. Inside the material the light is scattered by pigment grains, fibres and cells, and along the way certain wavelengths are absorbed. The fraction that comes back out, per colour, is the material's albedo — real objects average somewhere around 18% (SRC-095), snow much more, asphalt much less. Because the exit direction is essentially random, brightness does not change when you move: diffuse is view-independent (SRC-093).



Figure by Scratchapixel, What is Shading: Light-Matter interaction, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Source.
Compare the two bundles of arrows. Going in, on the right, red, green and blue are the same thickness — white light. Coming out, on the left, red and green are unchanged and the blue has been reduced to a hairline: the skin absorbed it. Red plus green added as light is the orange disc at the top left.
So the colour of an object is not something its surface adds. It is what is left of the lamp's light after the material has taken its cut, and it can only exist on this route — the arrows go in and out of the same patch of skin rather than bouncing off the top of it. Which is also why the highlight beside it is white: that light never went in, so nothing filtered it.


What it does depend on is how the surface faces the light. Turn a patch away from the lamp and the same beam spreads over more of it, so each square millimetre collects less. That is Lambert's cosine law, and it is why a sphere shades smoothly from bright to dark (SRC-095). The shading is glued to the geometry.
Route two, bouncing off. Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (SRC-094). That light spent no time inside the material, so no pigment ever filtered it: it keeps the light source's colour, not the object's. And with one outgoing direction per incoming one, the highlight slides across the surface as you move. Specular is view-dependent.
So the specular highlight moves when you move; the diffuse shading does not. That one test tells you whether a bright patch is a highlight or a light-coloured piece of paint, and it costs nothing but a head movement.



Figure by Scratchapixel, Reflection, Refraction and Fresnel, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Source.
Sunlight on rippled water: the specular route run a few thousand times at once, with the result of each test visible separately. Every white star is one patch of surface tilted so that its mirror direction happens to point at the camera. The plain dark blue between the stars is the same water under the same sun, failing that test by a degree or two.
Nothing in the pattern belongs to the water. Move the camera and a different set of patches lights up; hold still and the ripples travel, so it reshuffles anyway. And every glint is the same colour — white, the sun's, not the sea's — because each one is a small picture of the source.


What you can see in the picture



Stuart Kerr, Multi Colour Pool Balls in Triangle, 2009. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
Fifteen different diffuse colours; fifteen identical white specular highlights, each in the same place on its ball. The orange 5, the yellow 9 and the green 14 agree about nothing except their highlights — because the highlight belongs to the lamp, not to the ball. Each is a hard-edged little rectangle with a smaller glint beside it, repeated identically fifteen times: two rectangular sources somewhere above the table. Cross-check that against the shadows, as in Hard and soft light. The red cloth is close to pure diffuse — not a glint anywhere on it, just its own colour.


Most surfaces do both. Glossy paint, plastic, varnished wood, wet skin: coloured body plus a whitish highlight on top. PBRT sorts real surfaces into diffuse, glossy specular, perfect specular and retroreflective, and notes that most actual materials are a mixture (SRC-091).

Across different media


Almost all diffuse: Sánchez Cotán, c. 1602
Specular does the work: Kalf, 1656


Two still lifes lit the same way — one strong source from the left, a dark surround — sorted by which route dominates.
Sánchez Cotán chose objects that are nearly all diffuse: quince skin, cabbage leaf, cut melon, dressed stone. Track the melon — brightest where it faces the light, darkening smoothly round the curve, and nowhere a bright spot of a different colour from the melon. The one glossy object is the cucumber, and it carries the picture's only real highlight.
Kalf chose the opposite. On the silver ewer the diffuse route is gone entirely (see Metal and everything else) and what is left is a contorted picture of the room. On the lemons both routes run at once: hold on the front one and you get yellow body colour with a scatter of tiny white pinpricks over the pitted skin, in the colour of the light, not of the lemon.
Juan Sánchez Cotán, Still Life with Quince, Cabbage, Melon and Cucumber, c. 1602, and Willem Kalf, Still Life with a Silver Jug and a Porcelain Bowl, 1656. Both public domain.


The old workshop instruction to lay in the local colour first and add the highlight last, in a different, cooler, unmixed paint, is this physics restated as a procedure — painters who tint the highlight with the object's colour get clay instead of plastic. Photographers get at the same split with a polarising filter, which cuts specular reflection and leaves diffuse mostly intact: it kills glare on water, leaves and paint without changing their colour much. And nearly every renderer exposes the two routes as separate controls, a base colour or albedo map against a specular or roughness set (SRC-091).
Common mistakes

"Matte means rough, shiny means smooth." Not the same axis. Scratchapixel is explicit: what makes a material diffuse is usually its internal structure trapping and re-scattering light, not the roughness of its outer face (SRC-093). Chalk and a polished snooker ball are both smooth; one is nearly all diffuse, the other has a hard highlight on top of its diffuse colour.
"The highlight is the brightest part of the object's colour." It is not the object's colour at all. It is a picture of the lamp.
"Perfectly matte surfaces exist." They are a useful fiction. PBRT points out a perfectly diffuse surface is not physically realisable; dull chalkboard and matte paint are the closest real things (SRC-091).
"If it has no highlight it must be matte." It may just be angled so that no light source's mirror direction reaches the camera. Check other objects in the frame.


Reading a surface in five seconds

Find a bright patch. Is it the colour of the object, or of the light? Object colour means diffuse. Light colour means specular.
Look at the shape of the highlight. Does it match the source you can infer from the shadows — round sun, rectangular window, strip of tubes?
Do the highlights on every object in the frame agree about where the light is? A highlight on the left of one object and the right of another means two sources or two images.
If you have a second view of the same object, check that the highlight moved and the shading did not.
Anything with a highlight the same colour as its own body is either metal or wrong — go to Metal and everything else.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Metal and everything else
              Metals have almost no colour of their own and show you the room instead; everything else gets its colour from underneath and reflects the light's own colour on top. This is the sharpest material test you can run on an image.
            
          
        
          
            
              Roughness and Fresnel
              Two dials that finish a material. Roughness decides how blurry the reflection is; Fresnel makes every surface more reflective at glancing angles. Between them they explain why real objects are never evenly shiny.
            
          
        
          
            
              Hard and soft light
              Whether shadows have crisp edges or fade gradually. It is decided by one thing — how big the light looks from where the subject is standing.
            
          
        
          
            
              How to look at an image
              A repeatable way to see what an image is actually doing, instead of only noticing whether you like it.
